subject: chemistry-2
question: A student adds pure water to 50 mL of a 2 M solution until the total volume is 250 mL. What happens to the amount of solute and the concentration, and what is the new molarity?

options.text: Moles of solute decrease and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 0.4 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 0.4 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration is unchanged; the new molarity is 2 M
Moles of solute are unchanged and concentration decreases; the new molarity is 10 M

explanation:
Dilution adds solvent only, so the number of moles of solute is conserved while the volume rises, which lowers the concentration. Applying M1V1 = M2V2 gives M2 = (2 M)(50 mL) / 250 mL = 0.4 M. Choice D pairs the correct concept with the inverted ratio (2 x 250 / 50), and choice A misstates conservation of solute. The constancy of moles is precisely what makes the dilution equation valid, since M1V1 and M2V2 are both expressions for the same quantity of solute.

ELI-10: Adding water changes only the denominator of the concentration ratio. The solute particles already in the flask are not created or destroyed; you simply give them more room, so the number per liter falls. Check the direction before you trust the arithmetic: the volume went from 50 mL to 250 mL, five times larger, so the concentration must be one-fifth of 2 M, which is 0.4 M. A diluted solution that came out more concentrated than the original is always a signal that the ratio was flipped.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
